questions.text: Where does glycolysis take place?
questions.explain: Glycolysis is a cytosolic pathway that runs entirely in the cytoplasm. In contrast, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation take place in the mitochondria. This spatial separation allows both pathways to be regulated independently. Glycolysis remains active in the cytosol even under anaerobic conditions.

questions.text: How much energy is released during ATP hydrolysis?
questions.explain: The hydrolysis of one phosphoanhydride bond of ATP releases approximately −31 kJ/mol under standard conditions. This value explains why ATP is considered the universal energy carrier of the cell. The free energy arises from electrostatic repulsion between phosphate groups and resonance stabilization of the resulting ADP and inorganic phosphate. Under cellular conditions the actual value can be even higher.

questions.text: What distinguishes aerobic from anaerobic glycolysis?
options: The further fate of the pyruvate produced
The number of ATP molecules consumed
The number of reaction steps completed
questions.explain: Glycolysis itself proceeds identically in both cases and ends with pyruvate. The key difference lies in the further fate of pyruvate: aerobically it is imported into mitochondria and decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA. Anaerobically, pyruvate is reduced to lactate in the cytosol by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD⁺.

questions.text: What product is formed during the anaerobic breakdown of pyruvate in the cytosol?
questions.explain: Under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). In the process, NADH is reoxidized to NAD⁺, which is essential for glycolysis to continue. Lactate is released into the blood and can be converted back to glucose in the liver via the Cori cycle. Clinically, lactate rises during hypoxia, sepsis, and intense exercise.

questions.text: What is the correct net balance of glycolysis?
options: Glucose + 2 NAD⁺ + 4 ADP + 2 Pᵢ → 2 Pyruvate + 2 NADH + 4 ATP + 2 H₂O
Glucose + 2 NAD⁺ + 2 ADP + 2 Pᵢ → 2 Pyruvate + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H₂O
Glucose + 2 ADP + 2 Pᵢ → 2 Pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 CO₂
questions.explain: The net balance of glycolysis yields 2 ATP (4 produced minus 2 consumed in phase 1), 2 NADH, and 2 pyruvate per glucose. The NADH can supply additional ATP in the electron transport chain under aerobic conditions. Important: no CO₂ is produced in glycolysis — CO₂ is only released during oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate.

questions.text: Which three enzymes are considered the key regulatory enzymes of glycolysis?
options: Phosphoglycerate kinase, triose phosphate isomerase, enolase
questions.explain: The three key enzymes of glycolysis catalyze irreversible, highly exergonic reactions and are the main targets of regulation. Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate; PFK-1 is the most important regulatory enzyme; pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final ATP-producing step. All three are subject to allosteric and hormonal control.

questions.text: By which substance is phosphofructokinase 1 allosterically activated?
questions.explain: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the strongest allosteric activator of PFK-1 and a central regulatory molecule. It is produced by PFK-2, whose activity is hormonally controlled: insulin promotes, glucagon inhibits PFK-2 activity. ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1 (energy surplus), while AMP and ADP activate it.

questions.text: Which hormone inhibits the transcription of hexokinase?
questions.explain: Glucagon signals low blood glucose and inhibits transcription of glycolytic enzymes such as hexokinase. Insulin has the opposite effect and increases their expression. This hormonal control of gene expression allows long-term adaptation of the glycolytic rate to nutritional status. Glucagon simultaneously promotes gluconeogenesis in the liver.

questions.text: What does the Cori cycle describe?
options: Synthesis of glucose from amino acids in the muscle
Regeneration of NAD⁺ via the citric acid cycle in the liver
Breakdown of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA in the liver
Conversion of lactate to glucose between muscle and liver
Transport of pyruvate from the cytosol into mitochondria
questions.explain: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced during anaerobic muscle metabolism is transported via the blood to the liver. There it is converted back to glucose by gluconeogenesis (2 lactate → 1 glucose), which is made available to the muscle again. The cycle costs net energy (6 ATP equivalents per glucose) and occurs mainly during intense physical exercise.

questions.text: Which statement about the regulation of pyruvate kinase is correct?
options: It is allosterically activated by citrate
It is allosterically inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Insulin inhibits expression of the pyruvate kinase gene
It is allosterically inhibited by AMP
questions.explain: Pyruvate kinase is stimulated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate in a feedforward activation: when PFK-1 is active and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate accumulates, pyruvate kinase is pre-activated. It is inhibited by ATP and alanine (energy surplus or sufficient amino acids). Insulin increases expression of the pyruvate kinase gene — the opposite of option D.

questions.text: What distinguishes glucokinase from hexokinase?
options: Glucokinase is found in erythrocytes, hexokinase in the liver
Glucokinase has a lower Km for glucose than hexokinase
Glucokinase is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of fructose
Glucokinase consumes GTP instead of ATP in the reaction
questions.explain: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) is found mainly in the liver and pancreatic beta cells. It has a high Km (low affinity) for glucose, is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, and is induced by insulin. These properties make it the glucose sensor of the liver: it only becomes active at high blood glucose and adapts phosphorylation to supply.

questions.text: Which combination allosterically inhibits phosphofructokinase 1?
questions.explain: High ATP levels signal energy surplus and inhibit PFK-1 to slow down glycolysis. Citrate, a citric acid cycle intermediate, also inhibits PFK-1 and signals that the cell has sufficient biosynthetic precursors. In contrast, AMP and ADP (energy deficit) and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate PFK-1.

questions.text: How many ATP molecules are produced directly and net in glycolysis?
options: 4 ATP, since four molecules are formed in phase 3
1 ATP, since only one substrate-level phosphorylation step exists
6 ATP, since the NADH contribution is included
2 ATP, since two are consumed in phase 1 and four are formed in phase 3
8 ATP, since glucose contains six carbon atoms
questions.explain: In phase 1 (investment phase) 2 ATP are consumed (hexokinase and PFK-1). In phase 3 (payoff phase) 4 ATP are formed (2 × phosphoglycerate kinase and 2 × pyruvate kinase). The net gain is therefore 2 ATP per glucose. The NADH produced yields additional ATP under aerobic conditions — but only in the electron transport chain, not in glycolysis itself.

questions.text: In which clinical condition is an elevated blood lactate level most likely?
options: Elevated insulin levels after a meal
Tissue hypoxia in shock or severe sepsis
questions.explain: In tissue hypoxia (e.g. shock, sepsis, cardiac arrest) the electron transport chain cannot oxidize NADH sufficiently, causing increased reduction of pyruvate to lactate. This leads to lactic acidosis. A lactate > 2 mmol/L is a clinical warning value; values > 4 mmol/L indicate increased mortality risk. Regular lactate measurements are therefore standard in intensive care medicine.

questions.text: What is the end product of phase 1 of glycolysis?
questions.explain: Phase 1 of glycolysis (investment phase) encompasses the conversion of glucose to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate consuming 2 ATP. Key enzymes are hexokinase (step 1) and phosphofructokinase 1 (step 3). The resulting fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is cleaved in phase 2 by aldolase into two C3 units: glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP) and dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP).

questions.text: Where does gluconeogenesis mainly take place?
options: In skeletal muscle and the brain
In adipose tissue and the spleen
In cardiac muscle and the small intestine
In the lung and bone marrow
questions.explain: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the liver, which accounts for up to 90% of new glucose synthesis. The kidney contributes especially during prolonged fasting and acidosis. Other organs such as muscle or brain cannot perform significant gluconeogenesis because they lack key enzymes (e.g. glucose-6-phosphatase).

questions.text: What are the three main precursor substrates for gluconeogenesis?
options: Fatty acids, cholesterol and ketone bodies
questions.explain: The main substrates for gluconeogenesis are lactate (from anaerobic glycolysis, Cori cycle), glucogenic amino acids (e.g. alanine from muscle breakdown during fasting), and glycerol (from lipolysis in adipose tissue). Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose in humans because acetyl-CoA cannot enter gluconeogenesis.

questions.text: Why can gluconeogenesis not simply run glycolysis in reverse?
options: Because different coenzymes are needed in the reverse direction
Because glucose cannot be phosphorylated in the liver
Because NADH is not available for the reverse reaction
Because three glycolytic reactions are thermodynamically irreversible
Because pyruvate cannot be transported into mitochondria
questions.explain: Three glycolytic reactions are irreversible under physiological conditions: the reactions of hexokinase, phosphofructokinase 1, and pyruvate kinase. These must be bypassed in gluconeogenesis by specific circumventing reactions with their own enzymes. The remaining seven glycolytic reactions are reversible.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes the first step of gluconeogenesis starting from pyruvate?
questions.explain: Pyruvate carboxylase is located in the mitochondria and catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate consuming HCO₃⁻. It requires biotin as a cofactor. Acetyl-CoA is an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase — a signal that sufficient substrates for the citric acid cycle are available and excess pyruvate should be redirected into gluconeogenesis.

questions.text: In which cellular compartment is oxaloacetate converted to PEP by PEP carboxykinase?
options: In the intermembrane space of mitochondria
questions.explain: PEP carboxykinase (PEPCK) is a cytosolic enzyme that converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) and CO₂ consuming GTP. Since oxaloacetate cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, it is first reduced to malate, transported to the cytosol, and reoxidized to oxaloacetate there before PEPCK converts it to PEP.

questions.text: Which gluconeogenesis enzyme is localized in the endoplasmic reticulum?
questions.explain: Glucose-6-phosphatase is localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and catalyzes the final step of gluconeogenesis: removal of the phosphate group from glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose. Only the liver and kidney possess this enzyme, which explains why only these organs can release glucose into the blood. Its absence causes Von Gierke disease.

questions.text: What is the correct energy balance for gluconeogenesis forming 1 glucose from 2 pyruvate?
options: Consumption of 2 ATP and 2 GTP, no NADH required
Consumption of 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH
Consumption of 6 ATP and 2 FADH₂, no GTP required
Consumption of 2 ATP and 4 NADH, no GTP required
Consumption of 8 ATP and 4 GTP, 4 NADH required
questions.explain: Gluconeogenesis from 2 pyruvate requires: 2 ATP for pyruvate carboxylase, 2 GTP for PEPCK, 2 ATP for phosphoglycerate kinase (reverse), and 2 NADH for the reverse of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. The total balance is 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH — far more energy than glycolysis produces. Gluconeogenesis is driven by glucose shortage, not by energy surplus.

questions.text: What allosterically stimulates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase?
questions.explain: Citrate activates fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and simultaneously inhibits PFK-1 — a classic example of reciprocal regulation. High citrate levels signal that the citric acid cycle is saturated and glucose should be stored rather than burned. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, in contrast, inhibit the bisphosphatase and activate PFK-1 to drive glycolysis during energy deficit.

questions.text: What mechanism drives gluconeogenesis when lactate rises in the blood?
options: Law of mass action: higher substrate concentration drives the reaction toward glucose
Allosteric activation of pyruvate carboxylase by lactate
Hormonal induction of PEPCK by lactate directly
Activation of glucose-6-phosphatase by elevated lactate
Inhibition of glycolysis by lactate via PFK-1
questions.explain: Gluconeogenesis is regulated by substrate availability (law of mass action): when blood concentrations of lactate, alanine, or glycerol rise, gluconeogenesis is driven purely by chemical equilibrium without hormonal intervention. In the Cori cycle, muscle supplies lactate that is directly used for glucose synthesis in the liver.

questions.text: How does glucagon influence gluconeogenesis at the hormonal level?
options: Glucagon inhibits gluconeogenesis by activating FOXO1
Glucagon inhibits PEPCK gene expression via cAMP
Glucagon increases PEPCK gene expression via cAMP and CREB
Glucagon activates insulin receptors in hepatocytes
Glucagon stimulates glycolysis and inhibits gluconeogenesis
questions.explain: Glucagon binds to its G-protein-coupled receptor in hepatocytes and increases intracellular cAMP levels. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the transcription factor CREB. Phosphorylated CREB increases transcription of PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase. Cortisol acts synergistically via the glucocorticoid receptor. This induction takes hours to days.

questions.text: How does insulin inhibit gluconeogenesis at the molecular level?
options: Insulin activates CREB and increases PEPCK transcription
Insulin directly inhibits pyruvate carboxylase by contact
Insulin activates FOXO1 and increases PEPCK expression
Insulin lowers cAMP directly by inhibiting adenylate cyclase
Insulin phosphorylates and inactivates FOXO1, which otherwise promotes PEPCK
questions.explain: Insulin activates the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, which leads to phosphorylation of the transcription factor FOXO1 by Akt (PKB). Phosphorylated FOXO1 exits the nucleus and can no longer promote transcription of PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase. FOXO1 in its active (unphosphorylated) state is thus a promoter of gluconeogenesis — insulin shuts it off by phosphorylation.

questions.text: Which statement about Von Gierke disease (type 1a) is correct?
options: The cause is a defect in fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
The cause is a defect in glucose-6-phosphatase
The cause is a defect in pyruvate carboxylase
The cause is a defect in PEP carboxykinase
The cause is a defect in lactate dehydrogenase
questions.explain: Von Gierke disease type 1a is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by a defect in glucose-6-phosphatase in the ER. Without this enzyme, glucose-6-phosphate can be converted to free glucose neither from gluconeogenesis nor from glycogen breakdown. Consequences include severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly from glycogen accumulation, lactic acidosis, and elevated uric acid and triglyceride levels.

questions.text: Why cannot fatty acids contribute to gluconeogenesis in humans?
options: Because fatty acids cannot reach the mitochondria
Because fatty acid breakdown does not generate ATP
Because fatty acids are directly oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O
Because acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to oxaloacetate or PEP
Because fatty acids competitively inhibit pyruvate carboxylase
questions.explain: β-oxidation of fatty acids ends in acetyl-CoA. In the citric acid cycle, acetyl-CoA is completely oxidized to CO₂ — there is no net gain of oxaloacetate or other C4 compounds that could feed into gluconeogenesis. Therefore fatty acids are not gluconeogenic substrates. Glycerol (from triglycerides) can however enter gluconeogenesis as glycerol-3-phosphate.

questions.text: In which condition is gluconeogenesis most strongly activated?
options: Prolonged fasting with high glucagon and cortisol levels
During intense anaerobic muscle work alone
With high insulin levels and full glycogen stores
On an exclusively fat diet without protein intake
questions.explain: During prolonged fasting, glucagon and cortisol are chronically elevated. Glucagon induces transcription of PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase via cAMP/CREB; cortisol acts synergistically. Simultaneously, muscle proteolysis (alanine) and lipolysis (glycerol) provide ample substrate. Insulin is suppressed, so FOXO1 remains active and gluconeogenic enzymes stay upregulated.

questions.text: Which drug inhibits gluconeogenesis and is used as first-line therapy in type 2 diabetes?
questions.explain: Metformin is the most widely prescribed oral antidiabetic worldwide. It inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, raising the AMP/ATP ratio and activating AMPK. AMPK phosphorylates and inactivates CREB coactivators (PGC-1α/TORC2), thereby reducing transcription of PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase. The result is a marked reduction in hepatic gluconeogenesis.

questions.text: Which enzyme adds glucose residues to the non-reducing end of glycogen?
questions.explain: Glycogen synthase elongates glycogen chains by adding UDP-glucose to the non-reducing ends via α(1→4) glycosidic bonds. It requires a pre-existing glycogen primer (minimum 4 residues) or the protein glycogenin as initiator.

questions.text: What is the activated form of glucose used in glycogen synthesis?
questions.explain: Glucose must be activated to UDP-glucose by UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase before it can be incorporated into glycogen. The UTP used in this reaction is hydrolyzed to UMP + PPi; subsequent pyrophosphatase activity drives the reaction forward.

questions.text: Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves glycogen by:
questions.explain: Glycogen phosphorylase performs phosphorolysis: it uses inorganic phosphate (Pi) to cleave α(1→4) bonds at non-reducing ends, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. This is energetically favorable since glucose-1-phosphate is already phosphorylated, saving one ATP compared to hydrolysis.

questions.text: Von Gierke disease (GSD type I) results from a deficiency of:
questions.explain: Von Gierke disease is caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Without this enzyme, the liver cannot release free glucose into the blood from either glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis. This leads to severe fasting hypoglycemia and massive hepatic glycogen accumulation.

questions.text: Which hormone activates glycogenolysis in the liver via a cAMP-dependent pathway?
questions.explain: Glucagon binds its GPCR on hepatocytes → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA activation → phosphorylase kinase activation → glycogen phosphorylase activation. Simultaneously, PKA phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase, preventing futile cycling.

questions.text: The debranching enzyme has two catalytic activities. Which pair is correct?
questions.explain: The debranching enzyme first transfers a trisaccharide unit from a branch to the main chain (transferase activity), then hydrolyzes the remaining single glucose at the branch point (glucosidase activity), releasing free glucose rather than glucose-1-phosphate.

questions.text: McArdle disease (GSD type V) is characterized by muscle cramps during exercise due to deficiency of:
questions.explain: McArdle disease results from deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase. Muscle cannot mobilize glycogen during exercise, leading to energy failure, painful cramps, and myoglobinuria. Blood lactate fails to rise after forearm ischemic exercise — a classic diagnostic test.

questions.text: Glycogen synthase is maximally active in its:
questions.explain: Glycogen synthase is active (a-form) when dephosphorylated and inactive (b-form) when phosphorylated. Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis by activating protein phosphatase 1 (PP1), which dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase.

questions.text: Which protein acts as a primer for glycogen synthesis by accepting the first glucose residues?
questions.explain: Glycogenin is a self-glucosylating protein that forms the primer for glycogen synthesis. It attaches the first glucose to a tyrosine residue, then extends the chain to ~8 residues before glycogen synthase takes over.

questions.text: Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis by activating which phosphatase that dephosphorylates glycogen synthase?
questions.explain: Insulin signaling activates PP1 through Akt-mediated phosphorylation of its regulatory subunit. PP1 then dephosphorylates glycogen synthase (activating it) and glycogen phosphorylase (inactivating it), coordinately promoting glycogen synthesis.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes the condensation reaction that initiates the TCA cycle?
questions.explain: Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA (2C) with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C). This is the entry point of the TCA cycle. The enzyme is regulated by the energy status of the cell: inhibited by ATP, NADH, and succinyl-CoA.

questions.text: How many NADH molecules are produced per complete turn of the TCA cycle?
questions.explain: Three NADH molecules are produced per turn: at isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase. One FADH₂ is also produced at succinate dehydrogenase, and one GTP at succinyl-CoA synthetase.

questions.text: Which TCA cycle intermediate is a key precursor for heme synthesis?
questions.explain: Succinyl-CoA condenses with glycine (catalyzed by ALA synthase, requiring pyridoxal phosphate) to form δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first committed step of heme biosynthesis. This reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.text: Which TCA cycle enzyme directly produces GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.explain: Succinyl-CoA synthetase (also called succinate thiokinase) couples the hydrolysis of the high-energy thioester bond in succinyl-CoA to the phosphorylation of GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP in some tissues).

questions.text: Thiamine (B1) deficiency impairs the TCA cycle by affecting which enzyme complex?
questions.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for both pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-KGDH). Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy and beriberi due to impaired energy metabolism in high-demand tissues.

questions.text: Succinate dehydrogenase is unique among TCA cycle enzymes because it is:
options: Embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (Complex II)
Associated with the outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.explain: Succinate dehydrogenase is the only TCA enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is identical to respiratory chain Complex II — it oxidizes succinate to fumarate, reducing FAD to FADH₂, which feeds electrons directly into the ubiquinone pool.

questions.text: Which reaction is generally considered the rate-limiting step of the TCA cycle under most physiological conditions?
questions.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is a key regulatory enzyme. It is allosterically activated by ADP and Ca²⁺ and inhibited by ATP and NADH. By controlling flux at this step, the TCA cycle is coordinated with the cell's energy demands.

questions.text: If oxaloacetate (OAA) is depleted, which anaplerotic reaction can replenish it directly?
questions.explain: Pyruvate carboxylase is the primary anaplerotic enzyme in the liver: pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → OAA. It is activated by acetyl-CoA — a signal that acetyl-CoA is available but OAA is limiting, ensuring continued TCA cycle flux.

questions.text: Citrate exported from mitochondria to the cytosol is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase to provide acetyl-CoA for:
questions.explain: Citrate transport to the cytosol is the primary mechanism for exporting mitochondrial acetyl-CoA for biosynthesis. ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate into acetyl-CoA + OAA. This cytosolic acetyl-CoA is used for fatty acid synthesis and cholesterol (via HMG-CoA) synthesis.

questions.text: Which TCA cycle step involves an oxidative decarboxylation producing CO₂ and NADH?
questions.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the first oxidative decarboxylation: isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate + CO₂ + NADH. A second oxidative decarboxylation occurs at α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH).

questions.text: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) requires five coenzymes. Which combination correctly names all of them?
options: PLP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NADP⁺
TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FMN, NAD⁺
TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺
Biotin, lipoic acid, AMP, FAD, NAD⁺
questions.explain: PDH consists of three catalytic subunits: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase, uses TPP), E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, uses lipoic acid and CoA), and E3 (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, uses FAD and NAD⁺). All five coenzymes are essential; loss of any one arrests the entire complex.

questions.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH) are often discussed together. Which statement best describes what they genuinely share?
options: Both use biotin and transfer a carboxyl group to a mobile carrier between subunits
Both are cytosolic and regulated by reversible phosphorylation via insulin-sensitive kinases
Both differ in E1 specificity but share an identical E2 dihydrolipoyl transacylase subunit
Both produce acetyl-CoA as their acyl-CoA product and share the same E1 substrate pocket
Both are E1/E2/E3 complexes using the same five coenzymes to catalyze oxidative decarboxylation
questions.explain: PDH and OGDH share the same three-component architecture (E1/TPP, E2/lipoic acid+CoA, E3/FAD+NAD⁺) and catalyze analogous oxidative decarboxylation reactions — PDH converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂, OGDH converts α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA + CO₂. Their E3 subunit (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) is in fact identical, so a single E3 deficiency impairs both complexes simultaneously.

questions.text: High concentrations of which metabolite simultaneously inhibit citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-KGDH, slowing the TCA cycle when reducing equivalents are in excess?
options: NADH — accumulates when electron transport is saturated; direct product inhibitor at all three enzymes
ADP — signals low energy charge; acts as activator of isocitrate dehydrogenase and citrate synthase
Ca²⁺ — enters mitochondria during muscle contraction; activates isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-KGDH, and PDH phosphatase
Succinyl-CoA — direct product inhibitor of α-KGDH; downstream feedback inhibitor of citrate synthase
Acetyl-CoA — accumulates during β-oxidation; inhibits PDH but not all three TCA regulatory enzymes
questions.explain: NADH accumulation signals a high-energy, high-reduction state and inhibits all three major control points of the TCA cycle simultaneously. This product inhibition slows the cycle until NADH is re-oxidized by the respiratory chain. Ca²⁺ has the opposite effect — it activates the cycle during muscle activity — while ADP activates (not inhibits) isocitrate dehydrogenase.

questions.text: FADH₂ produced by succinate dehydrogenase yields fewer ATP than NADH. What is the primary mechanistic reason?
options: FADH₂ reaches Complex I at a later binding site than NADH, reducing the number of protons pumped per pair
FADH₂ has a more negative reduction potential than NAD⁺/NADH and cannot reduce ubiquinone without an additional energy input
FADH₂ is protein-bound in Complex II and passes electrons directly to ubiquinone, completely bypassing Complex I
FADH₂ donates to Complex III via a dedicated flavin carrier, skipping both Complex I and Complex II
FADH₂ is oxidized on the intermembrane-space face, reducing the effective proton gradient for ATP synthase
questions.explain: NADH feeds electrons into Complex I, which pumps 4 H⁺ per electron pair → ~2.5 ATP. FADH₂ is covalently bound to succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) and transfers electrons directly to ubiquinone, bypassing Complex I entirely — no proton pumping occurs at that step, yielding only ~1.5 ATP. The entry point into the respiratory chain is the decisive difference between the two carriers.

questions.text: Succinyl-CoA synthetase generates one GTP per turn of the human TCA cycle. What is the primary metabolic fate of this mitochondrial GTP?
options: Hydrolyzed by mitochondrial GTPase; energy phosphorylates AMP to ADP via unusual two-step transphosphorylation
Stored in matrix as regulatory signal activating GTP-dependent kinases for organelle dynamics
Exported via adenine nucleotide translocator to activate cytosolic GTP-binding signaling proteins
Converted to ATP by nucleoside diphosphate kinase: GTP + ADP → GDP + ATP
Used by ATP synthase as alternative substrate, producing ATP without the proton gradient
questions.explain: NDP kinase catalyzes the freely reversible reaction GTP + ADP ⇌ GDP + ATP, making the TCA-derived GTP energetically equivalent to one ATP. GTP can also directly power cytosolic reactions — notably gluconeogenesis, where PEPCK uses GTP to convert OAA to phosphoenolpyruvate — underscoring its dual role as energy currency and metabolic signal.

questions.text: Which complex of the respiratory chain accepts electrons from ubiquinol (QH₂) and passes them to cytochrome c?
questions.explain: Complex III (ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase) accepts electrons from ubiquinol and transfers them to cytochrome c via the Q cycle mechanism, simultaneously pumping 4 protons per 2 electrons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.text: The proton gradient generated by the respiratory chain is used by ATP synthase (Complex V) via:
questions.explain: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, the proton-motive force (electrochemical gradient) generated by the respiratory chain drives protons back through the F₀ subunit of ATP synthase. This proton flow drives rotation of the c-ring, causing conformational changes in the F₁ subunit that synthesize ATP.

questions.text: Cyanide is a potent inhibitor of cellular respiration because it blocks:
questions.explain: Cyanide (CN⁻) binds to the Fe³⁺ form of cytochrome a3 in Complex IV, preventing electron transfer to O₂. This halts the entire electron transport chain, collapses the proton gradient, and stops ATP synthesis. Tissues with highest O₂ demand (brain, heart) are most vulnerable.

questions.text: How many ATP molecules are produced per NADH oxidized in oxidative phosphorylation (using the P/O ratio of ~2.5)?
questions.explain: The modern estimate of the P/O ratio for NADH is ~2.5 ATP per NADH (not the classic '3' from older texts). This accounts for the actual H⁺/ATP stoichiometry of ATP synthase (~8 protons per 3 ATP) and the energy cost of ATP/ADP transport.

questions.text: Uncoupling proteins (UCPs) in brown adipose tissue dissipate the proton gradient as:
questions.explain: UCP1 (thermogenin) allows protons to leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without driving ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton-motive force as heat. This is the basis of non-shivering thermogenesis in newborns and cold-adapted mammals.

questions.text: Which mobile electron carrier shuttles electrons between Complex I/II and Complex III?
questions.explain: Ubiquinone (CoQ/Q) is a lipid-soluble molecule that diffuses within the inner mitochondrial membrane, collecting electrons from Complex I and II (as QH₂) and delivering them to Complex III. Cytochrome c is the water-soluble carrier between Complex III and IV.

questions.text: Rotenone, used as a pesticide and fish poison, inhibits the respiratory chain by blocking:
questions.explain: Rotenone blocks the transfer of electrons from the iron-sulfur clusters of Complex I to ubiquinone. It inhibits NADH oxidation without affecting succinate oxidation (Complex II). Rotenone is also used experimentally to model Parkinson's disease pathology.

questions.text: The final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial respiratory chain is:
questions.explain: Molecular oxygen (O₂) is the terminal electron acceptor. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) transfers electrons from cytochrome c to O₂, reducing it to water. This irreversible step drives the entire electron transport chain forward.

questions.text: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthesis by blocking:
options: The F₀ proton channel of ATP synthase
questions.explain: Oligomycin binds to the F₀ subunit of ATP synthase, blocking the proton channel. This prevents proton re-entry and ATP synthesis. Because the proton gradient cannot be dissipated, it also secondarily inhibits the respiratory chain.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the P/O ratio for FADH₂?
questions.explain: FADH₂ (generated at succinate dehydrogenase) donates electrons to ubiquinone, bypassing Complex I. Since Complex I pumps ~4 protons, bypassing it reduces the proton gradient contribution. The P/O ratio for FADH₂ is approximately 1.5 ATP.

questions.text: Cytosolic NADH from glycolysis cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which shuttle predominates in heart and liver, preserving the full ~2.5 ATP yield?
options: Malate-aspartate shuttle — regenerates NADH in the matrix; ~2.5 ATP
Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle — feeds electrons into Complex II; only ~1.5 ATP
Citrate shuttle — exports acetyl-CoA equivalents for cytosolic lipid synthesis
Carnitine shuttle — transports fatty acyl-CoA across the inner membrane
Pyruvate carrier — imports pyruvate into the matrix; no NADH transfer
questions.explain: The malate-aspartate shuttle uses malate dehydrogenase and aspartate aminotransferase on both membrane sides to funnel cytosolic NADH-equivalent reducing power into the matrix as NADH, entering at Complex I (~2.5 ATP). The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle is faster but less efficient (~1.5 ATP, Complex II entry) and predominates in brain and skeletal muscle. The citrate, carnitine, and pyruvate carriers serve entirely different transport functions.

questions.text: The Q cycle in Complex III results in net pumping of 4 H⁺ per 2 electrons. Which feature directly causes this amplification?
options: Both electrons from QH₂ bypass the Rieske centre and flow directly to cytochrome b
Rieske accepts both electrons from QH₂ and donates them to two cytochrome c molecules
QH₂ first reduces FMN in the matrix before electrons reach cytochrome c
Cytochrome b conformational changes drive proton pumping without any semiquinone
QH₂ oxidation bifurcates: one electron to cytochrome c via Rieske, one to Qi-site semiquinone
questions.explain: At the Qo site, QH₂ loses its two electrons along separate paths: one travels via the Rieske [2Fe-2S] cluster and cytochrome c₁ to cytochrome c (high-potential chain), while the other passes through cytochrome b (bL → bH) to a ubiquinone at the Qi site, generating a semiquinone. A second QH₂ oxidation completes this to QH₂ at the Qi site, releasing 2 H⁺ to the matrix. This bifurcation effectively doubles proton translocation per electron pair reaching cytochrome c, yielding 4 H⁺/2e⁻ net.

questions.text: What is the specific role of the Rieske iron-sulfur protein in Complex III?
options: Accepts electrons from QH₂ at the Qo site and passes them to cytochrome c₁
Accepts electrons from NADH at the matrix face and transfers them via FMN to ubiquinone
Accepts electrons from cytochrome c and passes them to the copper centres of Complex IV
Donates electrons directly to O₂, generating superoxide at the Qo site
Transfers electrons from succinate dehydrogenase to ubiquinone at the Qi site
questions.explain: The Rieske protein contains a [2Fe-2S] cluster with an unusually high reduction potential (~+0.28 V), placing it between ubiquinol and cytochrome c₁ in the high-potential branch of the Q cycle. At the Qo site it accepts one of the two electrons from QH₂ and donates it to cytochrome c₁, which then reduces soluble cytochrome c. Physical movement of the Rieske head domain between cytochrome b and cytochrome c₁ is essential for the bifurcated electron transfer.

questions.text: FMN is the primary electron acceptor from NADH in Complex I. Which statement correctly describes its function?
options: Accepts electrons from ubiquinol; transfers them back to NAD⁺ in the matrix
Acts as the final electron sink in Complex I; stays reduced when PMF is low
Accepts electrons from succinate dehydrogenase FADH₂; relays them to Fe-S clusters
Accepts 2e⁻ from NADH at once; passes them individually through Fe-S clusters to CoQ
Pumps protons from matrix to IMS directly; no iron-sulfur cluster involvement
questions.explain: FMN is a two-electron acceptor that receives both electrons from NADH simultaneously, forming FMNH₂. It then re-donates them one at a time to a series of iron-sulfur clusters (N1a, N3, N1b, N4, N5, N6a/b, N2), which are obligate single-electron carriers. Electron flow through this chain is coupled to conformational changes that pump 4 H⁺ per NADH. This two-to-one electron conversion is FMN's defining role in Complex I.

questions.text: In Boyer's binding-change mechanism, the proton-motive force does not directly form the ATP bond. What is its actual role?
options: Donates a proton directly to the β-phosphate of ADP to drive bond formation
Opens a channel in F₁ allowing free ATP and ADP diffusion across the inner membrane
Drives electron transfer in F₁ that activates ADP toward inorganic phosphate
Generates NADPH in the matrix to supply energy for ATP bond formation
Drives c-ring rotation, turning the γ-subunit; β-subunit conformational changes release bound ATP
questions.explain: ATP actually forms spontaneously (ΔG ≈ 0) at the tight catalytic site of F₁ — bond formation itself requires no external energy. The proton-motive force drives rotation of the F₀ c-ring, which turns the γ-subunit inside F₁, cycling each of the three β-subunits through open → loose → tight conformations. The energy-requiring step is the transition from tight to open, which releases the newly formed ATP. This rotary catalysis was confirmed by Boyer and Walker, Nobel Prize 1997.

questions.text: What is the thermodynamic driving force that moves electrons along the respiratory chain from NADH to O₂?
options: The NADH/NAD⁺ concentration gradient across the inner membrane
The ΔE°' between NADH/NAD⁺ (−0.32 V) and O₂/H₂O (+0.82 V)
The mechanical rotation of ATP synthase pulling electrons toward Complex IV
The transmembrane pH gradient acidifying the IMS to drive electron transfer
The high cytochrome c concentration in the IMS acting as a permanent electron sink
questions.explain: Electron flow in the respiratory chain is driven by the difference in standard reduction potentials. The NADH/NAD⁺ couple has E°' = −0.32 V; the O₂/H₂O couple has E°' = +0.82 V, giving ΔE°' = +1.14 V overall. By ΔG°' = −nFΔE°', this corresponds to ~−220 kJ per mol of electron pairs — a large spontaneous free energy change that drives electrons from Complex I through to Complex IV, coupling to proton pumping at each step.

questions.text: Strictly speaking, what is the direct product of the respiratory chain before ATP synthase acts on it?
options: ATP — via substrate-level phosphorylation at each electron transfer step
NADPH — regenerated by mitochondrial transhydrogenase using electron-flow energy
An electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force) across the inner membrane
Heat — thermal energy released as electrons fall through the complexes
Reduced cytochrome c — accumulates in the IMS when ATP synthase is inhibited
questions.explain: The respiratory chain's sole direct output is the proton-motive force (PMF), built up by pumping H⁺ from the matrix to the IMS at Complexes I, III, and IV. The PMF has two components: membrane potential (ΔΨ ≈ 150–180 mV, the dominant term in mitochondria) and a pH gradient (ΔpH ≈ 0.5–1 unit). ATP synthase then consumes this PMF to drive phosphorylation. Crucially, the PMF can also power active transport and heat production via UCPs — ATP synthesis is secondary.

questions.text: Where does β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids primarily occur?
questions.explain: β-Oxidation of long-chain fatty acids occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. Fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA in the cytosol, transported across the inner mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine shuttle, and then undergo successive rounds of β-oxidation.

questions.text: Which transport system is required to move long-chain acyl groups into the mitochondrial matrix?
questions.explain: Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly. CPT-I (outer membrane) converts acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine, which is transported by carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase and reconverted to acyl-CoA by CPT-II (inner membrane).

questions.text: How many rounds of β-oxidation are needed to completely oxidize palmitoyl-CoA (C16:0)?
questions.explain: Palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) requires 7 rounds of β-oxidation to produce 8 acetyl-CoA molecules. Each round shortens the chain by 2 carbons and produces 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH + 1 acetyl-CoA.

questions.text: Which enzyme is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, thereby regulating entry of fatty acids into mitochondria?
questions.explain: CPT-I is allosterically inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the first committed intermediate of fatty acid synthesis. This ensures that fatty acid synthesis and oxidation are not simultaneously active — when malonyl-CoA is high, CPT-I is inhibited and fatty acids are not transported into mitochondria.

questions.text: What products are generated in each cycle of β-oxidation?
questions.explain: Each round of β-oxidation produces: 1 FADH₂ (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step), 1 NADH (L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step), and 1 acetyl-CoA (thiolase step). These feed into the respiratory chain and TCA cycle respectively.

questions.text: During β-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids, which additional enzyme is required for double bonds in the cis configuration?
questions.explain: Unsaturated fatty acids with double bonds at odd-numbered carbons (cis-Δ³) require enoyl-CoA isomerase to convert cis-Δ³-enoyl-CoA to the trans-Δ²-enoyl-CoA that is the normal β-oxidation substrate. Double bonds at even-numbered carbons require 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase.

questions.text: In which organelle does β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (>C22) primarily occur?
questions.explain: Very-long-chain fatty acids are first shortened by β-oxidation in peroxisomes to medium-chain fatty acids, which are then transferred to mitochondria for complete oxidation. Peroxisomal β-oxidation produces H₂O₂ (detoxified by catalase) rather than pumping protons.

questions.text: What is the net ATP yield from the complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (C16:0)?
questions.explain: Palmitoyl-CoA oxidation yields 7 rounds × (1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH) + 8 acetyl-CoA. Using modern P/O ratios: 7×1.5 + 7×2.5 + 8×10 = 10.5 + 17.5 + 80 = 108, minus 2 for activation = 106 ATP equivalent.

questions.text: Carnitine deficiency leads to impaired fatty acid oxidation. Which symptom is most expected?
options: Hyperlipidemia with muscle weakness and hypoglycemia
questions.explain: Without carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria for β-oxidation. This causes accumulation of fatty acids (hyperlipidemia), muscle weakness (impaired energy supply), and hypoglycemia (inability to spare glucose by fat oxidation). Ketone body synthesis is also impaired.

questions.text: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is dangerous during fasting because:
options: Fatty acids cannot be oxidized for energy, leading to hypoglycemia
questions.explain: MCAD deficiency prevents oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids. During fasting, when glucose is limited and fatty acid oxidation is critical, this leads to severe hypoglycemia. Ketogenesis is also impaired because acetyl-CoA supply from β-oxidation is reduced.

questions.text: Where does fatty acid synthesis primarily occur in the cell?
questions.explain: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol, catalyzed by fatty acid synthase (FAS). The building blocks (acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA) must be exported from the mitochondria as citrate, then cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase in the cytosol.

questions.text: What is the committed step of fatty acid biosynthesis?
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This is the committed, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis. ACC is activated by citrate (high energy/precursor supply) and inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA and by phosphorylation via AMPK.

questions.text: Which reducing cofactor is required by fatty acid synthase for the reductive steps?
questions.explain: Fatty acid synthase requires NADPH for the two reductive steps per elongation cycle (ketoreduction and enoylreduction). NADPH is supplied mainly by the pentose phosphate pathway and the malic enzyme reaction. This is why NADPH is the 'reducing power' for biosynthesis.

questions.text: What is the primary product released by fatty acid synthase (FAS) in mammals?
questions.explain: Mammalian FAS releases palmitate (C16:0) as the primary product. Further elongation to longer-chain fatty acids and desaturation occur in the endoplasmic reticulum by specific elongases and desaturases.

questions.text: How many molecules of malonyl-CoA are required to synthesize one molecule of palmitate from acetyl-CoA?
questions.explain: Palmitate (C16:0) is synthesized from 1 acetyl-CoA starter unit and 7 malonyl-CoA extender units. Each malonyl-CoA adds 2 carbons (after decarboxylation), contributing 14 carbons; the starter acetyl-CoA adds 2 more, totaling 16.

questions.text: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is allosterically activated by:
questions.explain: Citrate allosterically activates ACC by promoting its polymerization into the active filamentous form. High citrate signals an abundance of acetyl-CoA and energy, indicating conditions favorable for fat synthesis. Conversely, palmitoyl-CoA (end-product) and AMPK phosphorylation inhibit ACC.

questions.text: Which enzyme introduces the first double bond into saturated fatty acids in mammals, typically at the Δ9 position?
questions.explain: Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD) introduces a cis double bond at the Δ9 position, converting stearoyl-CoA (C18:0) to oleoyl-CoA (C18:1, Δ9). Mammals lack Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases, making linoleic acid (Δ9,12) and α-linolenic acid (Δ9,12,15) essential dietary fatty acids.

questions.text: The acyl carrier protein (ACP) in FAS holds intermediates via which type of linkage?
options: Thioester bond to a phosphopantetheine group
questions.explain: Growing fatty acid chains are covalently attached to ACP via a thioester bond to the phosphopantetheine prosthetic group (derived from CoA). This thioester bond has high group transfer potential and is essential for the condensation reactions catalyzed by FAS.

questions.text: Insulin stimulates fatty acid synthesis primarily by:
options: Activating a phosphatase that dephosphorylates and activates ACC
questions.explain: Insulin activates protein phosphatase 2A, which dephosphorylates ACC, activating it. Insulin also induces transcription of FAS and ACC genes, increases glucose uptake (providing acetyl-CoA and NADPH via glycolysis and PPP), and inhibits AMPK.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes why linoleic acid (18:2, Δ9,12) is an essential fatty acid?
options: Humans cannot synthesize fatty acids longer than C16
Humans lack the Δ12-desaturase needed to introduce the Δ12 double bond
Linoleic acid cannot be activated to acyl-CoA
β-Oxidation of linoleic acid is toxic
Linoleic acid is only found in animal fats
questions.explain: Mammals have desaturases for positions Δ9, Δ6, Δ5, and Δ4, but lack Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases. Therefore, linoleic acid (18:2 Δ9,12) and α-linolenic acid (18:3 Δ9,12,15) must be obtained from the diet and are classified as essential fatty acids.

questions.text: What is the first step in the catabolism of most amino acids?
questions.explain: The first step is usually removal of the amino group, either by transamination (transfer to α-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate) or oxidative deamination (glutamate dehydrogenase, releasing NH₄⁺). The resulting α-keto acid enters central metabolic pathways.

questions.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the cofactor for which type of enzyme central to amino acid catabolism?
questions.explain: PLP (vitamin B6 derivative) forms a Schiff base with amino acids at the active site of aminotransferases, enabling transfer of the amino group to α-ketoglutarate. PLP is also required for decarboxylases, racemases, and serine/threonine dehydratases.

questions.text: Phenylketonuria (PKU) results from a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. What accumulates as a result?
questions.explain: Without phenylalanine hydroxylase (which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine), phenylalanine accumulates and is shunted to phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, and phenyllactate (collectively 'phenylketones'). These are neurotoxic, causing intellectual disability if untreated.

questions.text: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by a deficiency in the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, which affects catabolism of:
questions.explain: The branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex oxidatively decarboxylates the α-keto acids derived from leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Deficiency causes accumulation of these keto acids, which give urine a sweet maple syrup odor and cause severe neurological damage.

questions.text: Which amino acid is the primary nitrogen carrier from peripheral tissues to the liver?
questions.explain: Alanine is the primary nitrogen carrier via the glucose-alanine cycle: muscle transaminates pyruvate with amino group from amino acid catabolism to form alanine, which travels to the liver. There, alanine transaminase regenerates pyruvate (for gluconeogenesis) and glutamate (enters urea cycle).

questions.text: Homocystinuria is associated with deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase. Which metabolic pathway is primarily affected?
questions.explain: Cystathionine β-synthase converts homocysteine + serine → cystathionine in the transsulfuration pathway. Deficiency causes homocysteine accumulation, leading to cardiovascular disease, lens dislocation, and intellectual disability. Vitamin B6, B12, and folate are used in treatment.

questions.text: Glucogenic amino acids can be converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis. Which of the following is purely glucogenic?
questions.explain: Alanine is purely glucogenic — it is transaminated to pyruvate, which can be converted to OAA (by pyruvate carboxylase) and then to glucose via gluconeogenesis. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic; phenylalanine and isoleucine are both glucogenic and ketogenic.

questions.text: The catabolism of phenylalanine and tyrosine ultimately produces which TCA cycle and ketone body precursors?
questions.explain: Phenylalanine is first hydroxylated to tyrosine. Tyrosine degradation proceeds through homogentisate → maleylacetoacetate → fumarylacetoacetate → fumarate + acetoacetate. This makes phenylalanine/tyrosine both glucogenic (fumarate → TCA → gluconeogenesis) and ketogenic (acetoacetate).

questions.text: Which vitamin B6-dependent reaction removes the amino group from glutamate, releasing free ammonium?
questions.explain: Glutamate dehydrogenase (in the mitochondrial matrix) catalyzes: glutamate + NAD⁺ → α-ketoglutarate + NADH + NH₄⁺. This is the major route for releasing free ammonia in the liver for urea synthesis. The enzyme can use either NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ and is regulated by ATP, GTP (inhibit) and ADP, GDP (activate).

questions.text: Alkaptonuria results from a defect in homogentisate oxidase. Which amino acids cannot be catabolized normally?
questions.explain: Homogentisate oxidase catalyzes a step in the degradation of phenylalanine and tyrosine. Its deficiency causes accumulation of homogentisic acid, which is excreted in urine (turns dark on standing) and deposits in connective tissues (ochronosis), causing arthritis.

questions.text: In which two compartments of the hepatocyte does the urea cycle operate?
questions.explain: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix (CPS-I and OTC), while the remaining three reactions (ASS, ASL, arginase) occur in the cytosol. Citrulline is exported from the mitochondria via a specific transporter to continue the cycle.

questions.text: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
questions.explain: CPS-I is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle. It condenses NH₃ + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate. It requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an allosteric activator, which is synthesized from acetyl-CoA + glutamate when amino acid load is high.

questions.text: N-Acetylglutamate (NAG) activates CPS-I. NAG is synthesized when amino acid catabolism increases, signaled by elevated levels of:
questions.explain: NAG synthase is activated by arginine and uses acetyl-CoA + glutamate as substrates. When amino acids are being catabolized in large amounts, glutamate (from transamination) and acetyl-CoA accumulate, stimulating NAG synthesis and thereby activating CPS-I.

questions.text: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder. Its X-linked inheritance means affected males present with:
questions.explain: OTC deficiency causes severe hyperammonemia in affected hemizygous males because carbamoyl phosphate cannot be transferred to ornithine and accumulates, overflowing into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway (producing orotic acid). Hyperammonemia causes cerebral edema and is often fatal neonatally.

questions.text: Which amino acid is regenerated at the end of each turn of the urea cycle, serving as a carrier?
questions.explain: Ornithine is regenerated by arginase, which cleaves arginine to urea + ornithine. Ornithine is then transported back into the mitochondria to react with carbamoyl phosphate again, acting as the catalytic carrier molecule of the cycle.

questions.text: Which nitrogen atom in urea comes from the direct addition of free ammonia (NH₄⁺) via CPS-I?
options: One nitrogen (from NH₃ via carbamoyl phosphate)
questions.explain: Urea contains two nitrogen atoms. One comes from free ammonia (NH₃) incorporated by CPS-I into carbamoyl phosphate. The second comes from the amino group of aspartate, which is incorporated at the argininosuccinate synthetase step. Fumarate is released when aspartate donates its amino group.

questions.text: Citrullinemia type I results from a deficiency of argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS). What accumulates in blood and urine?
questions.explain: ASS catalyzes citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinate. Its deficiency causes citrulline to accumulate dramatically in blood and urine (citrullinemia). Ammonia also rises because the urea cycle is blocked. Treatment includes protein restriction and sodium benzoate/phenylbutyrate.

questions.text: Fumarate produced in the urea cycle by argininosuccinate lyase is important because it:
options: Enters the TCA cycle, linking it to the urea cycle
Is converted to malate for gluconeogenesis only
Is converted to aspartate in the cytosol only
questions.explain: Fumarate released by argininosuccinate lyase enters the TCA cycle (fumarate → malate → OAA). OAA can be transaminated to aspartate, which then re-enters the urea cycle. This connection is called the 'urea cycle–TCA cycle bicycle' and links nitrogen disposal to energy metabolism.

questions.text: In hyperammonemia, which amino acid carries nitrogen from muscles to the liver for detoxification, and how?
options: Alanine — via the glucose-alanine cycle; also glutamine — via amidation of glutamate
Glycine — via the glycine cleavage system
questions.explain: Two main nitrogen carriers: (1) Alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) — muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine; liver extracts the amino group. (2) Glutamine — synthesized in muscle/brain by glutamine synthetase (fixes NH₃); released, taken up by liver and intestine, and deaminated by glutaminase.

questions.text: Arginase deficiency causes argininemia. What is the distinguishing neurological feature compared to other urea cycle defects?
options: Progressive spastic diplegia and intellectual disability rather than acute hyperammonemia
questions.explain: Arginase deficiency (argininemia) typically presents with progressive spastic diplegia and intellectual disability rather than life-threatening hyperammonemia, because alternative pathways can partially clear ammonia. Arginine accumulates and is believed to be neurotoxic. Ammonia elevation is milder than in other urea cycle disorders.

questions.text: What structural feature of water molecules enables them to form hydrogen bonds?
options: A bent geometry with partial negative charge on O and partial positive charges on H atoms
A linear geometry that maximizes dipole alignment
Equal electronegativity of H and O in the O–H bond
The presence of non-polar O–H bonds
A trigonal planar arrangement of electron pairs around oxygen
questions.explain: Water is a polar molecule with a bent geometry (~104.5°). Oxygen's high electronegativity creates a partial negative charge and two lone electron pairs, while hydrogen atoms carry partial positive charges. This polarity allows each molecule to form up to four hydrogen bonds: two as donor (via its H atoms) and two as acceptor (via the lone pairs on O). This extensive network explains water's anomalously high boiling point, surface tension, heat capacity, and solvent power.

questions.text: Which formula correctly defines pH?
questions.explain: pH is the negative decimal logarithm of the molar proton concentration. Because [H⁺] in pure water is 10⁻⁷ mol/L, pH = 7. Option C describes pOH; option D gives 14 (a constant, not a definition); option E is dimensionally incorrect.

questions.text: What is the ion product of water (Kw) at 25 °C?
questions.explain: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L² at 25 °C. In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L, hence pH = 7. Kw increases with temperature: at 37 °C it is ~2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴, meaning neutral pH at body temperature is closer to 6.8 — though blood is maintained at 7.35–7.45.

questions.text: A solution has [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol/L. What is its pH and character?
questions.explain: pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. A pH below 7 indicates an acidic solution ([H⁺] > [OH⁻]). Each unit change in pH reflects a 10-fold change in [H⁺], so pH 3 is 10,000× more acidic than pH 7.

questions.text: What does the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation describe?
options: The dependence of enzyme velocity on substrate concentration
The relationship between pH, pKa, and the ratio [A⁻]/[HA]
The temperature dependence of pKa values
The relationship between osmolarity and pH
The relationship between Kw and temperature
questions.explain: The equation is: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). It quantifies the pH of any buffer from its pKa and the ratio of conjugate base to acid. When [A⁻] = [HA], log(1) = 0 and pH = pKa — the buffering midpoint. Applied to blood: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻]/[dissolved CO₂]).

questions.text: At what pH does a weak acid with pKa = 4.8 exist 50% as HA and 50% as A⁻?
questions.explain: When [A⁻] = [HA], the logarithmic term in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation equals zero, so pH = pKa = 4.8. This is the buffering midpoint with maximal buffer capacity. Effective buffering occurs within ±1 pH unit of the pKa; outside this range one species predominates and buffer capacity collapses.

questions.text: Which is the most important extracellular buffer in blood?
questions.explain: The bicarbonate buffer system provides ~50% of total blood buffering capacity. Its pKa is 6.1, yet it is highly effective because the lungs continuously remove CO₂ (open system), keeping dissolved CO₂ low. The kidney adjusts [HCO₃⁻] over hours to days for long-term compensation. The normal [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃] ratio at blood pH 7.4 is approximately 20:1.

questions.text: What is the normal pH range of arterial blood?
questions.explain: Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35–7.45, slightly alkaline, maintained by buffer systems, pulmonary CO₂ control, and renal HCO₃⁻ regulation. Below 7.35 is acidemia; above 7.45 is alkalemia. Values outside 7.0–7.8 are incompatible with life.

questions.text: At what condition is the buffer capacity of a weak acid/base pair maximal?
options: When pH = pKa (equal concentrations of HA and A⁻)
When the solution is completely deprotonated (pH >> pKa)
When only the conjugate acid HA is present
questions.explain: Buffer capacity (β) is maximal at pH = pKa where HA and A⁻ are equimolar. Mathematically β = 2.303 × C × α(1 − α), maximized at α = 0.5. Effective buffering occurs within ±1 pH unit around the pKa; outside this range capacity decreases sharply.

questions.text: Which primary blood chemistry change characterizes metabolic acidosis?
options: Rise in pCO₂ with normal HCO₃⁻
Fall in pCO₂ with normal HCO₃⁻
Fall in pO₂ with normal HCO₃⁻
questions.explain: Metabolic acidosis is a primary reduction in plasma [HCO₃⁻] (< 22 mmol/L), pulling pH below 7.35. Causes include diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis (hypoxia, sepsis), renal failure, and severe diarrhea (HCO₃⁻ loss). Compensatory hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) lowers pCO₂ to partially restore the [HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂] ratio.

questions.text: A patient hyperventilates due to anxiety. Which acid-base disturbance develops?
questions.explain: Hyperventilation eliminates CO₂ faster than it is produced, lowering pCO₂ (hypocapnia). The equilibrium CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ shifts left, reducing [H⁺] and raising pH above 7.45 — respiratory alkalosis. Clinical signs include paresthesias and carpopedal spasm (reduced ionized Ca²⁺ at higher pH) and lightheadedness. Treatment: controlled breathing or CO₂ rebreathing.

questions.text: A patient's blood shows [HCO₃⁻] = 24 mmol/L and pCO₂ = 40 mmHg. Using pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × pCO₂)), what is the blood pH?
questions.explain: Dissolved CO₂ = 0.03 × 40 = 1.2 mmol/L. pH = 6.1 + log(24/1.2) = 6.1 + log(20) = 6.1 + 1.30 = 7.40. The normal [HCO₃⁻]/[dissolved CO₂] ratio of 20:1 always yields pH 7.4. The lung defends pCO₂; the kidney defends [HCO₃⁻]. This calculation is the basis of arterial blood gas interpretation.

questions.text: What is the thermodynamic driving force of the hydrophobic effect?
options: Electrostatic repulsion between nonpolar molecules and water
Entropy gain when ordered water cages around nonpolar groups are released into bulk water
Enthalpy gain from van der Waals bonds between hydrophobic molecules
Covalent bond formation between nonpolar groups
Entropy decrease when nonpolar molecules cluster together
questions.explain: Nonpolar molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with water and force surrounding water into a rigid, low-entropy cage. When hydrophobic groups cluster, these cages dissolve into disordered bulk water, releasing many water molecules and dramatically increasing system entropy (ΔS > 0). This entropy-driven process drives membrane bilayer formation, protein hydrophobic core burial, and ligand-receptor docking.

questions.text: Why does water far more effectively shield electrostatic interactions between ions compared with a nonpolar solvent?
options: Water increases ionic charges by proton transfer reactions
Water has a very high dielectric constant (~80), orienting its dipoles around ions and weakening coulombic forces
Water covalently binds to ions and neutralizes their charge
Water's low boiling point allows rapid ion exchange
Hydrogen bonds in water directly neutralize ionic charges
questions.explain: The relative permittivity (dielectric constant) ε of water at 25 °C is ~80 versus ~2 for hexane. Oriented hydration shells of water dipoles reduce the effective coulombic force between two charges by a factor of ε. This stabilizes charged and polar transition states in enzyme active sites, enables dissolution of salts, and allows biological polyelectrolytes (DNA, RNA) to exist in solution without self-aggregation.

questions.text: In which of the following reactions does water directly participate as a substrate?
options: Transfer of phosphate from ATP to glucose by hexokinase
Reduction of NAD⁺ to NADH by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
Hydrolysis of a peptide bond by a serine protease
Decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase
questions.explain: Serine proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase) cleave peptide bonds using water as the second substrate. The catalytic serine attacks the carbonyl carbon forming an acyl-enzyme intermediate; a water molecule then performs deacylation, regenerating the enzyme and releasing the C-terminal fragment. Water also participates in phosphatase reactions, DNA hydrolysis, and hundreds of other metabolic hydrolase reactions.

questions.text: What is the general structure shared by all 20 standard amino acids at physiological pH?
options: An α-carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and an R-group
A central carbon bearing two amino groups, a carboxyl group, and a hydrogen
A nitrogen atom bearing a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a variable side chain
A central carbon bearing one amino group, two carboxyl groups, and a variable side chain
A six-membered ring structure carrying both an amino and a carboxyl group
questions.explain: All standard amino acids share a central α-carbon bonded to: an amino group (–NH₃⁺ at pH 7), a carboxyl group (–COO⁻ at pH 7), a hydrogen atom, and a variable R-group (side chain). At physiological pH they exist as zwitterions — simultaneously carrying positive and negative charges. The R-group alone determines each amino acid's chemical identity and properties.

questions.text: What type of bond links amino acids in a polypeptide chain, and what structural feature restricts rotation around it?
options: An ester bond between the carboxyl and a hydroxyl group; rotation restricted by steric clashes
An amide (peptide) bond; planar due to resonance delocalization on the C–N bond
A phosphodiester bond as found in nucleic acids; restricted by the phosphate geometry
A hydrogen bond between adjacent carbonyl and amino groups along the backbone
A disulfide bond formed by oxidation of two adjacent cysteine thiol side chains
questions.explain: A peptide bond is an amide bond formed by condensation between the α-carboxyl of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next (–H₂O). Resonance delocalization gives the C–N bond ~40% double-bond character, making the six atoms of the peptide unit coplanar and rigid. Free rotation occurs only at the N–Cα bond (φ angle) and the Cα–C bond (ψ angle), which define backbone conformation.

questions.text: What defines the primary structure of a protein?
options: The three-dimensional fold of the polypeptide chain
The spatial arrangement of secondary structure elements
The linear sequence of amino acids from N- to C-terminus
The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits
The pattern of disulfide bonds between cysteine residues
questions.explain: Primary structure is the covalent sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, written N→C by convention. It is encoded by the gene and determined during ribosomal translation. All higher-order structure is determined by the primary sequence. Even a single substitution can be catastrophic: Val→Glu in β-globin causes sickle cell disease by promoting haemoglobin polymerization.

questions.text: Which statement best describes the α-helix?
options: A left-handed helix with 3.6 residues per turn, stabilized by hydrogen bonds between side chains
A right-handed helix with 3.6 residues/turn; backbone NH of residue i bonds to C=O of residue i+4
A structure built from alternating glycine and alanine residues stacked in rigid parallel sheets
Extended antiparallel strands joined by backbone hydrogen bonds perpendicular to the strand direction
A coiled coil of two α-helices wound around each other, stabilized by a hydrophobic interface
questions.explain: The α-helix is right-handed with 3.6 residues per turn and a rise of 0.15 nm per residue (pitch 0.54 nm). Each backbone N–H donates a hydrogen bond to the backbone C=O four residues earlier (i→i+4), running parallel to the helix axis. Side chains project outward. Proline disrupts α-helices at internal positions because it lacks a backbone NH and its ring fixes the φ angle.

questions.text: How are hydrogen bonds oriented in a β-pleated sheet?
options: Between side chains of residues within the same strand
Between backbone NH and C=O groups of residues i and i+4 within a single strand
Between backbone NH and C=O groups of adjacent parallel or antiparallel strands
Between Cα hydrogens of residues on opposite strands
Only between cysteine residues forming disulfide bonds across strands
questions.explain: In a β-sheet, extended strands are held laterally by inter-strand backbone hydrogen bonds between the NH of one strand and the C=O of an adjacent strand. In parallel β-sheets both strands run N→C; in antiparallel sheets they run in opposite directions, giving more linear (stronger) hydrogen bonds. Side chains alternate above and below the sheet plane.

questions.text: Which combination of forces primarily maintains the tertiary structure of a globular protein?
options: Covalent peptide bonds supplemented by covalent phosphodiester crosslinks between backbone residues
Disulfide bonds exclusively, since all non-covalent interactions are too weak to maintain structure
Hydrophobic interactions, H-bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals forces, and disulfide bonds
Direct covalent bonds between all adjacent side chains, forming a rigid and inflexible network
Exclusively van der Waals interactions between backbone atoms, with no contribution from side chains
questions.explain: Tertiary structure is stabilized by multiple forces acting cooperatively: the hydrophobic effect (burial of nonpolar residues — typically the dominant force), hydrogen bonds between polar side chains and backbone, ionic interactions (salt bridges), van der Waals contacts, and for extracellular proteins, covalent disulfide bonds. No single interaction is sufficient alone; denaturation occurs when their combined stabilization is overcome.

questions.text: What is quaternary protein structure?
options: The linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide
The three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide chain
The spatial arrangement of α-helices and β-sheets within one chain
The assembly of two or more polypeptide subunits into a functional complex
The pattern of post-translational modifications on amino acid side chains
questions.explain: Quaternary structure describes how multiple polypeptide chains (subunits) associate via non-covalent interactions (and sometimes disulfide bonds) to form a larger functional complex. Example: haemoglobin is an α₂β₂ tetramer. Not all proteins have quaternary structure — monomeric myoglobin does not. Subunit assembly can enable cooperativity and allosteric regulation.

questions.text: What is the isoelectric point (pI) of a protein?
options: The pH of maximum protein solubility
The pH at which the protein carries a net positive charge
The pH at which the net charge of the protein is zero
The pH at which all ionizable groups are fully protonated
The pH equal to the average pKa of all ionizable residues
questions.explain: At pH = pI, the sum of positive charges exactly equals the sum of negative charges (net charge = 0). Below pI the protein is net positive; above pI it is net negative. At pI, electrostatic repulsion between molecules is minimal, so solubility is lowest — the basis of isoelectric precipitation and isoelectric focusing (IEF) in 2D-gel electrophoresis.

questions.text: Why does proline disrupt α-helices at internal positions?
options: Its bulky aromatic ring system generates steric clashes with backbone atoms of adjacent residues
Its ring fixes the φ angle and removes the backbone NH needed for helix H-bonds
It carries a net negative charge at pH 7 that electrostatically repels the helix macrodipole
It spontaneously forms disulfide bonds that lock the backbone into a non-helical geometry
Its side chain competes with helix backbone C=O groups for the backbone NH hydrogen-bond donor
questions.explain: Proline's side chain is covalently bonded to its own backbone nitrogen, forming a five-membered pyrrolidine ring. This (1) constrains the φ angle to approximately −60°, and (2) eliminates the backbone N–H group, removing the hydrogen bond donor required for α-helix formation. Proline therefore acts as a helix breaker but is common at helix N-termini and in tight turns.

questions.text: What happens to a protein during denaturation?
options: Peptide bonds are hydrolyzed and free amino acids are released into solution
Secondary and higher-order structure is lost while the primary sequence remains intact
Only disulfide bonds are broken, leaving the secondary structure fully intact
The protein gains additional hydrogen bonds and becomes more ordered
Post-translational modifications are selectively cleaved from side chains
questions.explain: Denaturation disrupts non-covalent interactions (and sometimes disulfide bonds), unfolding secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure. The covalent peptide backbone is not broken, so the primary sequence is preserved. Denaturing agents include heat, extreme pH, urea/guanidinium chloride (disrupt H-bonds), and SDS (disrupts the hydrophobic core). Denaturation may be reversible (ribonuclease A) or irreversible (cooked egg white).

questions.text: What is the role of molecular chaperones in protein folding?
options: They synthesize the polypeptide chain by catalyzing peptide bond formation at the ribosome
They bind hydrophobic patches on unfolded chains, preventing aggregation
They tag misfolded proteins with ubiquitin and deliver them to the 26S proteasome for degradation
They thread unfolded polypeptides through membrane channels to reach their target organelle
They catalyze post-translational modifications including glycosylation and phosphorylation events
questions.explain: Molecular chaperones (e.g., Hsp70, GroEL/GroES, Hsp90) recognize exposed hydrophobic regions on nascent or stress-unfolded polypeptides, transiently binding them to prevent aggregation. ATP-driven binding and release cycles give the chain multiple opportunities to reach its native fold. Chaperones do not supply folding information — the native structure is determined solely by the amino acid sequence (Anfinsen's principle).

questions.text: Where do disulfide bonds form in proteins, and what prevents their formation in the cytoplasm?
options: In the cytoplasm, where reactive oxygen species drive oxidation of all exposed cysteine residues
In the ER lumen and extracellular space; the reducing cytoplasm (high GSH) prevents –S–S– formation
In the mitochondrial matrix, where they stabilize subunits of the electron transport chain
In the nucleus, where they crosslink adjacent histone octamers to compact chromatin structure
On the ribosome, where they join the nascent chain covalently to ribosomal RNA during translation
questions.explain: Disulfide bonds form by oxidation of two cysteine –SH groups (–S–S– + 2H). The endoplasmic reticulum lumen is oxidizing; the cytoplasm is highly reducing (~1–10 mM glutathione, GSH), keeping cysteines in the –SH state. Disulfide bonds stabilize secreted and extracellular proteins (antibodies, insulin, digestive enzymes) that must function in variable environmental conditions.

questions.text: What information does a Ramachandran plot convey?
options: The free energy change of protein folding as a function of temperature for each residue type
The sterically allowed φ/ψ backbone dihedral angle pairs for amino acid residues
The distribution of side-chain rotamer conformations observed in crystal structures
The correlation of protein molecular weight with sedimentation rate in ultracentrifugation
The geometry and pattern of backbone hydrogen bonds within a single α-helical repeat
questions.explain: The Ramachandran plot (1963) maps the sterically permitted combinations of φ (N–Cα bond) and ψ (Cα–C bond) backbone dihedral angles, derived from van der Waals clash criteria. Favored regions correspond to α-helix (~φ = −57°, ψ = −47°) and β-sheet (~φ = −120°, ψ = +120°). Glycine, lacking a Cβ, populates a much larger region; proline is confined to a narrow area. The plot is used to validate protein crystal structures.

questions.text: What is the defining structural feature of collagen that gives connective tissue its tensile strength?
options: A compact globular fold with a buried hydrophobic core and amphipathic helices at the surface
A Gly-X-Pro triple helix of three polyproline II-type chains wound into a right-handed superhelix
An antiparallel β-sheet with interchain disulfide bonds connecting every adjacent cysteine pair
A right-handed α-helix with covalent crosslinks between hydroxylysine and lysine of adjacent chains
A β-barrel whose hydrophobic lumen forms a protected channel for water and small-ion transport
questions.explain: Each collagen chain repeats Gly–X–Pro/Hyp. Three left-handed polyproline II-type helices coil into a right-handed superhelix stabilized by interchain hydrogen bonds. Glycine — the smallest amino acid — must occupy every third position to fit the sterically crowded interior of the triple helix. Hydroxyproline (formed by prolyl hydroxylase using vitamin C) is essential for this stability; vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy through defective collagen.

questions.text: What does Anfinsen's thermodynamic hypothesis (Anfinsen's dogma) state?
options: Correct folding always requires ATP-driven chaperones and cannot occur spontaneously for any protein
The native state has the highest free energy and is maintained by the kinetic barrier of disulfide bonds
The sequence encodes the fold; the native state is the global free energy minimum
The ribosome determines tertiary structure by geometrically constraining the emerging polypeptide chain
Secondary structure must fully assemble before any tertiary contacts can form in a strict hierarchy
questions.explain: Anfinsen showed (Nobel Prize 1972) that fully denatured ribonuclease A (unfolded with urea + β-mercaptoethanol) spontaneously refolded to full enzymatic activity upon removal of denaturants. This proved all information for correct folding is encoded in the primary sequence. The native state is the thermodynamically most stable (lowest free energy) structure. Chaperones assist kinetics in vivo but do not alter the thermodynamic endpoint.
